children: is urging its suppliers to embrace greater automation as the aircraft maker works to increase jet production and overcome persistent manufacturing bottlenecks.

Chief Technology Officer Lane Ballard said at an industry event Wednesday that aerospace manufacturing needs to rely less on labor-intensive processes such as hand riveting and make greater use of automation, software and autonomous systems. Suppliers will need to make the same transition to support Boeing’s planned production increases.
For investors, improving manufacturing efficiency is closely tied to Boeing’s
financial recovery. Higher 737 Max output could generate more cash, help the company reduce debt and allow it to compete more effectively with Airbus
in the single-aisle market. But achieving those benefits depends on Boeing
and its suppliers being able to raise production without creating new quality or supply-chain problems.
Boeing and Airbus are both trying to increase output to meet large order backlogs, while shortages of components and other supplier constraints have limited the pace of production.

CEO Kelly Ortberg said last week that stabilizing 737 production at 47 aircraft a month has taken longer than expected, with wing production among the challenges. He indicated that the supply chain should be capable of supporting the next production increase once Boeing
resolves remaining manufacturing-flow issues, which he expects next year.
Ballard said the industry will increasingly need engineers with expertise in software, artificial intelligence and autonomous systems as manufacturers redesign production around higher volumes.
The long-term demand backdrop remains substantial. Boeing
estimates the commercial aviation market will require about 40,000 new aircraft over the next two decades.

title: Boeing pushes suppliers toward automation as jet production ramps up
